title: The Treasure Nobody Wanted
summary: Alexander the Great comes to the land of King Katzia and sees a strange court case: two men are arguing, and each insists that the treasure found in a ruin belongs to the other. A funny, touching story about honesty, and about how honest people are the greatest treasure of all.
pages: A very long time ago there lived a great and mighty king named Alexander the Great. He traveled with a huge army to faraway lands and saw palaces, deserts and seas. But more than anything he wanted to know one thing: how do other kings judge their people?

One day Alexander came to a very faraway land, beyond the Mountains of Darkness. A king named Katzia ruled there. Katzia welcomed him with honor, seated him at a big table and served him a tray. And on the tray was bread… made of gold! Yellow, shining bread, hard as stone.

"What is this?" Alexander laughed. "I don't eat gold!"
"In that case," Katzia asked with a smile, "why did you come all the way to us? Was there no bread in your land?"
"I didn't come for your riches," Alexander answered. "I came to see how you judge."

Just then two men came into the palace. They looked very excited, and each of them talked fast-fast. "My lord the king, judge between us!" they asked. Alexander sat down and listened curiously. What were they fighting about? Money? Land?

The first man said: "I bought a ruin from this man, an old, broken-down house. I started clearing away the stones, and suddenly I found a treasure of gold coins! But I only bought the ruin, not the treasure. So the treasure is his, and I want to give it back to him. And he refuses to take it!"

The second man said: "When I sold him the ruin, I sold it with everything inside it. The treasure belongs to him, not to me! I won't take something that is no longer mine."
Alexander's mouth dropped open. He had heard many quarrels in his life, but never one like this: each one wants to give, and nobody wants to take!

King Katzia thought for a moment, then asked the first man: "Do you have a son?"
"Yes," the man answered.
And he asked the second: "And do you have a daughter?"
"Yes," the second answered.
"In that case," said Katzia, "let the son marry the daughter, and the treasure will belong to both of them."

The two men looked at each other and smiled a big smile. The son and the daughter got married, and there was a joyful wedding with both families. And the treasure? It stayed in the new family, and both fathers were pleased. No one took anything that wasn't his.

Alexander the Great sat quietly for a long time. He was a king who had conquered half the world, but now he felt he had learned something new. "I have seen a lot of gold on my travels," he said in wonder, "but honest people like these I have never seen. They are the most precious treasure."

And you? Have you ever found something that wasn't yours, a pencil at preschool, a ball in the playground or a coin on the sidewalk? What did you do? Sometimes it's hard to give things back. But like the two men in the story, we can choose honesty too, and feel truly rich, deep in our hearts.
